source.title: Rethinking Overlooked Aspects in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Yuan Liu; Le Tian; Xiao Zhou; Jie Zhou

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study varies vision-language pre-training data scale and reports benchmark results that qualify the expectation of predictable downstream gains: improvements are marginal and some results decline at larger data scales.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates benchmark performance, not held-out cross-entropy or fitted power-law curves. Its SFT dataset-selection and model-comparison results do not independently test the claim versions. Figure 2 contains additional plotted results, but exact values are not stated in the text and are not extracted as figure-only rows.
record.test_reason: The study scales vision-language alignment pre-training data (1M–100M LAION samples) and LLM size for LLaVA-style models, then reports downstream benchmark performance. That is a new setting with a result on V6. The authors explicitly contrast it with the LLM scaling-law expectation. It reports no loss and fits no power laws, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. The scaled data feeds only the adapter and vision-encoder alignment stage, not LLM pretraining, which narrows how far the result generalises.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that naively adding LAION image-caption pre-training data (1M–100M) gives little or no improvement and can degrade VLM performance. Gains come mainly from a larger LLM, not from parallel data growth. They attribute the flat data scaling to noisy data and to distribution overlap with the vision encoder's pretraining, and they call for better data quality and diversity. Separately, they propose Individual Select for SFT data.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies multimodal pre-training dataset size and evaluates downstream benchmarks; it does not fit or predict held-out language-model cross-entropy power laws or optimize allocations at fixed compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported performance varies with pre-training data scale; the paper notes deterioration beyond 50M in some cases and gives a 3.3-point SEED-Bench drop for Qwen1.5-7B from 20M to 100M.
record.problems: The scaling evidence is benchmark performance rather than held-out loss or fitted power laws; the text gives few exact values, no uncertainty estimates, and does not state the benchmark for the Vicuna size comparison. The plotted results are not numerically detailed in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 shows further per-model/per-benchmark plotted results, but the text does not state their exact values; these are not separately extracted. Other reported SFT ablations and model comparisons do not test the claim versions.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss; any fitted trend or extrapolation of downstream scores; scaling of LLM pretraining data or compute (only the alignment-stage data is scaled).
The power-law form in vision-language training is not tested: no loss is reported and no curve is fitted.

missing.what: Finding that the data-scaling trend is nearly the same across model sizes, so larger models do not benefit more from more alignment data (authors contrast this with LLMs)
Model-size comparisons at the default 558K pre-training: Yi-6B vs Yi-34B (MME 1772.8 vs 1840.3, MMB 70.4 vs 74.8) and Qwen1.5-7B vs 14B (MME 1657.4 vs 1801.7)
Per-model, per-benchmark values across the seven data splits

record.verdict_notes: The scaled 'pre-training' is the VLM alignment stage (adapter plus unfrozen vision encoder), followed by SFT. It is not LLM pretraining, so the challenge to V6 applies to this alignment-data axis only. No uncertainty estimates are given; the evidence rests on authors' descriptions of Figure 2 plus Table 1. The paper cites Hoffmann et al. as the LLM scaling law it contrasts against.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No fits on small runs or predictions of much larger runs are reported.
The study does not compare fixed-compute allocations or estimate compute-optimal parameter and token scaling.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.

The study investigates pre-training data scale in vision-language models, but reports benchmark performance rather than loss or a fitted power-law form; that measure does not test whether the same power-law form holds.

Tests downstream benchmark performance against pre-training data scale and model size in the reported vision-language setting; does not test predictability from pretraining loss or across other tasks and modalities.
No comparison of fitting choices, loss exponents, or fitted compute-optimal splits.

rows.note: Aggregate trend as described by the authors; exact per-model and per-benchmark values are only shown in Figure 2.
rows.check: State should be absent, not partial. The Figure 2 caption says performance 'remained nearly consistent, with some instances of degradation'. The text says gains are only 'marginal' over 1M→100M, two orders of magnitude. The subject list should read Yi-6B/34B: Table 1 uses Yi-6B, while the Figure 2 label says Yi-7B. Four benchmarks were used (MMBench, MME, SEED, ScienceQA), although the text says 'three'.

relationships.condition: LLaVA-1.5-style VLMs (Vicuna, Qwen1.5, Yi), alignment pre-training data scaled 1M→100M LAION samples, benchmark scores after SFT
relationships.reason: Performance stays nearly flat and declines beyond 50M, e.g. Qwen1.5-7B SEED-Bench falls 3.3 points from 20M to 100M (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Performance stayed nearly flat and declined beyond 50M samples, including a 3.3-point SEED-Bench decline for Qwen1.5-7B from 20M to 100M.

relationships.condition: Increasing LLM size within a family (Vicuna-7B→13B) at a fixed 1M alignment-data budget
relationships.reason: The larger LLM improves the benchmark by 3.0 points (R3). Table 1 shows similar gains for Yi-6B→34B and Qwen 7B→14B, not captured as rows.
relationships.display_finding: Scaling Vicuna from 7B to 13B improved the benchmark by 3.0 points, with similar gains reported for Yi and Qwen.

relationships.condition: Joint scaling of LLM size and alignment-data size
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not the rows: the trend across data scales is 'almost consistent' for every model size. Larger models gain nothing extra from more data, so the gains depend on which axis is scaled.
relationships.display_finding: Trends across alignment-data sizes were nearly consistent across model sizes, with larger models receiving no additional benefit from more data.
